what_its_for: Indapamide is a water pill (diuretic) used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to reduce fluid buildup (swelling/edema) in the body, especially in people with heart failure. Lowering high blood pressure helps prevent strokes, heart attacks, and kidney problems.
how_to_take: Take indapamide by mouth, exactly as your doctor prescribed. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food. Take it in the morning to avoid having to wake up at night to urinate. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
dosing: The usual starting dose for high blood pressure is 1.25 mg once daily in the morning. Your doctor may increase your dose to 2.5 mg or up to 5 mg once daily depending on how well it works for you. For fluid retention (swelling), the typical dose is 2.5 mg once daily in the morning. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same morning. If it is later in the day or almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time the following morning. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store indapamide at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and increase dizziness. Avoid getting up too quickly from sitting or lying down to prevent dizziness and falls. Avoid too much sun exposure or tanning beds, as indapamide can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and protective clothing. Avoid taking extra potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless your doctor approves. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking any over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen, as they can reduce how well indapamide works and may affect your kidneys.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe dizziness, fainting, or lightheadedness; signs of low potassium such as muscle cramps, weakness, or irregular heartbeat; signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, little to no urination, or dark-colored urine; a rash, itching, or difficulty breathing (signs of allergic reaction); numbness or tingling in hands or feet; unusual tiredness or confusion; or gout symptoms such as sudden severe joint pain. Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you have chest pain, difficulty breathing, or signs of a severe allergic reaction.
when_it_works: Indapamide starts working within 1 to 2 hours of taking a dose. However, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you notice a significant improvement in your blood pressure. The full benefit for blood pressure control may take up to 8 weeks. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel well, because high blood pressure often has no symptoms.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with extra caution, as you may be more sensitive to dizziness, falls, and electrolyte imbalances (low sodium or potassium). Stay well hydrated. Pregnancy: Indapamide is generally not recommended during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor right away if you become pregnant while taking this medication. Breastfeeding: It is not known if indapamide passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver disease: Use with caution. Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and electrolyte levels closely. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established; it is not typically used in children. Diabetes: Indapamide may affect your blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood sugar more closely and tell your doctor about any changes.
